name: Aluminum chloride prescription (Drysol)
lead: Drysol is a brand of prescription topical aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating.[1] People use it for a presentation payoff: less visible sweat on underarms, hands, feet or face means fewer sweat stains on clothes, drier handshakes and a neater look through the day. Aluminium chloride is a stronger version of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy.[1]

Wikipedia reports that improvement takes about three to five days and that the most common side effect is skin irritation.[1] Case reports describe 20% aluminium chloride in alcohol (Drysol) used for localized sweating, including a woman with one-sided segmental hyperhidrosis and a patient with facial and scalp sweating treated with it alongside an oral medicine.[4][5] Hyperhidrosis is described in the dermatology literature as a psychosocially embarrassing condition.[3]

Training forums such as T Nation have threads in which lifters ask about heavy sweating and share what they use, including moisture-wicking clothing and, in one thread, a link to consumer information on prescription aluminium chloride.[6][7][8]

paras: Hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8% of the US population, most often appearing between ages 25 and 64, with a family history in 30 to 50 percent of cases.[1] Higher-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants have shown some success for hand and foot sweating.[1]

Beyond underarm sweating, Drysol has been reported for palmar and plantar sweating,[1] localized one-sided sweating,[5] and facial and scalp sweating in combination with oral clonidine in a single case report.[4] Dermatologists have also used aluminium chloride (Drysol) as a hemostatic agent in minor surgical procedures.[10]
Skin irritation is the most common side effect.[1] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[2]

A 1978 case report described miliaria (heat rash) with exertion after repeated use of 20% aluminium chloride in a patient with segmental hyperhidrosis.[5] A 1993 report described an unusual histiocytic reaction in skin biopsies after topical aluminium chloride used as a hemostatic agent.[10]
Wikipedia cites Everdry as the first commercial antiperspirant in 1903.[2] Specific details about Drysol's development were not found in the sources loaded.

No controlled trials specific to Drysol appeared in the sources loaded. The published record consists of case reports,[4][5] a 1977 Medical Letter review titled 'Drysol for treatment of hyperhidrosis',[9] and the guideline summary in the Hyperhidrosis article, which cites an evidence-based review of nonsurgical management and guidance from the International Hyperhidrosis Society without giving trial results.[1] A case report on botulinum toxin for inguinal hyperhidrosis lists aluminium-salt antiperspirants such as Drysol among treatments of varied success.[3]

timeline.event: Everdry, the first commercial antiperspirant, marketed.[2]

quick.overview:
Drysol is a prescription aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis. It is a stronger form of the ingredient in ordinary antiperspirants.

Topical antiperspirants are guideline first-line treatment.
quick.mechanism: Aluminium salts block sweat ducts, reducing sweat output.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is the most common effect. Kidney dysfunction warrants a doctor consult per the FDA.

chain: Aluminium salts applied to sweat-prone skin
Sweat output at that site is reduced
Fewer sweat stains and less damp skin
angle.text: The solution reduces sweating where it is applied, which people use to avoid visible underarm marks, wet hands or a shiny face. The effect is on sweat rather than skin or body features.
